description: Spacelanders is a team of curious minds, builders, and explorers who combine science, engineering, and creativity to turn challenging ideas into practical solutions. For NASA Space Apps Challenge, we are developing SEAL — Sun–Earth Analysis for Landing, an interactive tool for exploring solar illumination and direct-to-Earth communication opportunities at lunar landing sites.

SEAL (Sun–Earth Analysis for Landing) is a browser-based tool for exploring lunar landing opportunities, with a focus on the Moon's south pole. By combining NASA/JPL Horizons ephemerides with lunar terrain data from LRO LOLA and WAC imagery, SEAL connects celestial geometry with the conditions a lander may encounter on the surface.

Our demo features an interactive 3D Moon, terrain shading, landing-site exploration, temporal charts, and timelines. Users can investigate solar illumination and Earth visibility, compare locations and dates, and explore how sunlight, battery capacity, and power consumption affect a lander's operating window.

SEAL addresses the challenge of understanding lunar landing conditions across both space and time. Local terrain, illumination, communication geometry, and energy constraints can make seemingly similar locations behave very differently.

By making these relationships visible and explorable, SEAL aims to support preliminary landing-site assessment, encourage scientific reasoning, and make the engineering challenges of lunar exploration more accessible. Ultimately, we want to help people understand not simply where humanity can land on the Moon, but when and under what conditions meaningful surface operations become possible.
details:
SEAL (Sun-Earth Analysis for Landing)

The Moon is not equally hospitable everywhere, nor at every moment. At its south pole, sunlight, terrain, and communication geometry create a particularly demanding environment for exploration. A landing site's coordinates alone cannot tell the whole story. We must also understand how its surrounding terrain and celestial conditions shape what is possible, and how those conditions change over time.

SEAL (Sun–Earth Analysis for Landing) is a browser-based tool for exploring lunar landing opportunities. Our mission is to connect lunar geography with the environmental conditions that shape surface operations, helping users understand not only where a lander might go, but when and under what conditions it could operate.

In our current demo, users can select candidate or historical landing sites, choose a date, and explore when the Sun and Earth appear above the local horizon. They can compare locations, follow environmental changes over time, and investigate how sunlight, battery capacity, and power consumption influence a lander's operating window. An interactive three-dimensional Moon, terrain shading, charts, and timelines bring otherwise abstract astronomical relationships into a tangible, exploratory experience.

SEAL combines NASA/JPL Horizons ephemerides with lunar elevation data from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter's Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) and imagery from its Wide-Angle Camera (WAC). Three.js powers the lunar visualization, while Chart.js supports analytical charts. Built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, the application runs as a static website, making lunar environmental exploration accessible directly through a browser.

Our approach is grounded in a simple observation: a landing site is not merely a location. It is a location at a particular moment, under a particular sky, surrounded by terrain that can change what is possible. Local ridges can interrupt sunlight or obstruct communication with Earth. Darkness introduces power constraints. Favourable conditions must therefore be understood not only by their presence, but also by their timing, duration, and relationship to operational needs.

These considerations shaped both our scientific scope and engineering decisions. We considered terrain coverage and resolution, available ephemeris date ranges, geometric visibility versus terrain obstruction, simplified power-system assumptions, and the need for responsive performance in a browser. Rather than pursuing unnecessary computational or graphical complexity, we focused on connecting essential environmental variables through an accessible analytical interface.

What makes SEAL distinctive is its emphasis on space and time together. It brings location, illumination, communication geometry, and operational constraints into a shared environment where their relationships can be explored rather than treated as isolated datasets. This transforms lunar landing assessment from simply identifying a destination into examining the opportunities and limitations surrounding it.

SEAL aims to make the challenges of lunar exploration tangible and understandable. For aspiring mission planners and researchers, it provides an environment to investigate how location, timing, illumination, communication, and energy availability interact. For students and educators, it turns complex astronomical datasets into an experience that encourages exploration, experimentation, and scientific reasoning. For the broader public, it offers a window into the engineering decisions behind humanity's return to the Moon.

Our longer-term ambition is to support more informed preliminary landing-site assessment by making environmental trade-offs easier to visualize and compare. We hope SEAL can inspire a more analytical approach to lunar exploration, where the question is not simply where humanity can land, but where conditions can sustain meaningful operations.

Ultimately, SEAL seeks to bridge the distance between scientific data and human understanding-making the conditions for operating on another world something people can explore, reason about, and appreciate.

We are building SEAL to turn the Moon from a map of possible destinations into a landscape of possible opportunities.
